富曰教而已庶而不富則無以厚民生富而不教則
無以正民德斯誠治道之不可闕者君人者於此有
失得而治效之隆替隨之故自昔守成之君夏有啓
商有高宗周有成康降是而下則僅有漢文帝誠如
聖策之所云者然較諸古之帝王則其德之醇疵治之大
小不能無所分辨而
聖心嘗慕之者所謂聞一善言見一善行沛然若決江河
而况善之在文帝其可取者尤非止於一端也觀其
===
席高祖新造之基啓西京近古之治家無不給人無
不足而殷富之效臻吏安其官民樂其業而醇厚之
風作兵革庶乎不試刑辟幾於弗用所以然者蓋不
惟其時為守令於郡縣者尚寬平而崇德化亦以其
修於身而後施諸天下凡治本之所存治具之所出
咸槩得之故其宮室苑囿車騎服御稍有不便輙弛
以利民欲作露臺召匠計直一聞百金之費則惜而
不為衣則弋綈也履則革舃也集囊為帷也編蒲為
席也所幸夫人衣不曳地也治霸陵皆瓦器不得以
金銀銅鐵為飾也欲厚風俗則止嗇夫之拜除誹謗
punctuated: 君師而無慊也。三復敬嘆之餘，敢不竭其愚衷而對揚萬一乎？臣惟天生斯民，立之司牧，而寄以三事：曰庶，曰富，曰教而已。庶而不富，則無以厚民生；富而不教，則無以正民德。斯誠治道之不可闕者。君人者於此有失得，而治效之隆替隨之。故自昔守成之君，夏有啓，商有高宗，周有成康；降是而下，則僅有漢文帝，誠如聖策之所云者。然較諸古之帝王，則其德之醇疵、治之大小，不能無所分辨。而聖心嘗慕之者，所謂聞一善言，見一善行，沛然若決江河。而況善之在文帝，其可取者尤非止於一端也。觀其席高祖新造之基，啓西京近古之治，家無不給，人無不足，而殷富之效臻；吏安其官，民樂其業，而醇厚之風作；兵革庶乎不試，刑辟幾於弗用。所以然者，蓋不惟其時為守令於郡縣者尚寬平而崇德化，亦以其修於身而後施諸天下，凡治本之所存、治具之所出，咸槩得之。故其宮室苑囿、車騎服御，稍有不便，輒弛以利民。欲作露臺，召匠計直，一聞百金之費，則惜而不為。衣則弋綈也，履則革舄也，集囊為帷也，編蒲為席也，所幸夫人衣不曳地也，治霸陵皆瓦器，不得以金銀銅鐵為飾也。欲厚風俗，則止嗇夫之拜，除誹謗
translation_en:
…to be ruler and teacher without inadequacy. Having read these words repeatedly with reverent admiration, how could I fail to exhaust my humble sincerity in responding to even a ten-thousandth part of your intent?

Your servant considers that Heaven brought forth these people and established rulers to shepherd them, entrusting them with just three tasks: increasing their numbers, enriching them, and educating them. If the people become numerous but are not enriched, there is no means to sustain their livelihood; if they are enriched but not educated, there is no means to rectify their moral character. These are indeed indispensable elements of the Way of government. As rulers succeed or fail in these matters, the achievements of their government flourish or decline accordingly. Thus, among rulers of old who maintained an inherited realm, the Xia had Qi, the Shang had Gaozong, and the Zhou had Cheng and Kang. After them there was scarcely anyone but Emperor Wen of the Han, exactly as Your Majesty’s policy question states. Yet, when he is compared with the emperors and kings of antiquity, distinctions must be drawn concerning the purity or flaws of his virtue and the greater or lesser scope of his government. Your Majesty’s longstanding admiration for him exemplifies the saying that, on hearing a single good word or seeing a single good deed, one responds with an irresistible surge, like the Yangzi or Yellow River bursting its banks. Moreover, the admirable qualities of Emperor Wen were far from confined to one respect.

Consider how he built upon the foundations newly laid by Gaozu and inaugurated a government under the Western Han that approached that of antiquity. Every household was provided for, and every person had enough: the results of abundant prosperity were achieved. Officials were secure in their offices, and the people took pleasure in their occupations: an atmosphere of simple integrity arose. Weapons were scarcely put to the test, and punishments were almost unused. This was not merely because the prefects and magistrates then serving in the commanderies and counties esteemed leniency and fairness and honored moral transformation. It was also because he cultivated himself before extending his influence throughout the realm, broadly grasping both the foundations of government and the sources of its practical means.

Thus, whenever his palaces, parks, carriages, mounts, clothing, or other personal provisions caused even a slight inconvenience, he dispensed with them for the people’s benefit. Wishing to build an open terrace, he summoned craftsmen to estimate its cost; once he heard that it would require a hundred units of gold, he begrudged the expense and abandoned the project. He wore dark, coarse silk [?] and leather shoes; he made curtains from gathered sacks [?] and mats from woven rushes. Even the robes of his favored consort did not trail on the ground. In preparing his tomb at Baling, he used only earthenware vessels and prohibited ornaments of gold, silver, copper, or iron. Wishing to improve popular customs, he halted the appointment of a bailiff and abolished the prohibition on criticism …

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
之法欲恤民隱則今年議振貸明年減田租詔舉賢
良而求直言之士躬耕籍田以先務本之民時有獻
千里馬者輒下詔却而不受陳武建征伐之議則曰
念不到此也賈生陳改正朔易服色定官名之請則
曰未遑也即此類而推之則其時宗廟非無祭祀之
禮也百官非無俸給之需也四夷非無征伐之費也
上有節儉之君下無侈靡之習儲蓄於公私者取之
不窮應辦夫緩急者度其可繼田租雖除用度自給
無可疑者不然何貢助徹之法雖三代亦所常行而
漢乃有蠲賦之年哉我
===
太祖高皇帝備自古帝王之德膺
上天曆數之歸汛掃胡元輯寧中夏尺地莫非其有一民
莫非其臣
列聖相承
仁恩四洽百二十餘年生齒之繁疆域之廣益加于前
漢唐方亨之際晉宋未遷之先莫盛於
今日者仰惟
陛下蒞阼之初廣離照之明奮乾綱之斷威福作于惟辟
政事修以及時刑獄不頗而法吏無私名器不濫而
士風以正罷無名之征斂停不急之造作革奢僭之

今日者仰惟
陛下涖阼之初廣離照之明奮乾綱之斷威福作于惟辟
政事修以及時刑獄不頗而法吏無私名器不濫而
士風以正凡無名之征歛停不急之造作革耆僧之
punctuated:
之法。欲恤民隱，則今年議振貸，明年減田租；詔舉賢良而求直言之士，躬耕籍田以先務本之民。時有獻千里馬者，輒下詔却而不受。陳武建征伐之議，則曰：「念不到此也。」賈生陳改正朔、易服色、定官名之請，則曰：「未遑也。」即此類而推之，則其時宗廟非無祭祀之禮也，百官非無俸給之需也，四夷非無征伐之費也。上有節儉之君，下無侈靡之習，儲蓄於公私者取之不窮，應辦夫緩急者度其可繼。田租雖除，用度自給，無可疑者。不然，何貢、助、徹之法雖三代亦所常行，而漢乃有蠲賦之年哉？
我太祖高皇帝備自古帝王之德，膺上天曆數之歸，汛掃胡元，輯寧中夏。尺地莫非其有，一民莫非其臣。列聖相承，仁恩四洽，百二十餘年。生齒之繁，疆域之廣，益加于前。漢唐方亨之際，晉宋未遷之先，莫盛於今日者。仰惟陛下蒞阼之初，廣離照之明，奮乾綱之斷，威福作于惟辟，政事修以及時，刑獄不頗而法吏無私，名器不濫而士風以正。罷無名之征斂，停不急之造作，革奢僭之
translation_en:
…the law [against defamatory speech]. Wishing to relieve the people’s hardships, he deliberated on relief grants and loans one year and reduced the land tax the next. He issued edicts recommending the worthy and good and sought men who would speak frankly; he personally plowed the imperial ritual field to lead the people in pursuing agriculture, the fundamental occupation. Whenever someone presented a horse capable of traveling a thousand li, he issued an edict declining it. When Chen Wu proposed military campaigns, he said, “My thoughts do not extend to this.” When Master Jia proposed changing the calendrical reckoning and the colors of official dress and establishing official titles, he said, “I have not yet had leisure for this.”
From such examples we may infer that ancestral temples at that time still required sacrificial ceremonies, the officials still needed their salaries, and campaigns against the peoples of the four quarters still entailed expenditure. Yet above there was a frugal ruler, and below there were no habits of extravagance. Public and private reserves could be drawn upon without exhaustion, and provision for ordinary and urgent needs was calculated to ensure that it could be sustained. Although the land tax was abolished, resources naturally sufficed for expenditure: there is no room for doubt. Otherwise, why were the gong, zhu, and che systems of taxation regularly practiced even under the Three Dynasties, while the Han nevertheless had years in which taxes were remitted?
Our Emperor Taizu Gao possessed all the virtues of the emperors and kings of antiquity and received the succession ordained by High Heaven. He swept away the alien Yuan and brought peace to the central lands. Not a foot of land was outside his possession; not a single person was outside his subjecthood. Successive sage sovereigns inherited the throne, their benevolence and favor reaching everywhere for more than 120 years. The population’s numbers and the territory’s extent have grown beyond those of earlier times. Neither the Han and Tang at the height of their prosperity nor the Jin and Song before their southward transfers surpassed the flourishing condition of today.
I reverently reflect that, from the beginning of Your Majesty’s accession, you extended the brilliance symbolized by the trigram Li and exercised the resolve symbolized by the governing power of Qian. Punishment and reward proceeded from the sovereign alone; affairs of government were attended to in due season. Criminal proceedings were impartial, and judicial officials showed no favoritism; titles and insignia of office were not bestowed indiscriminately, and the conduct of scholars was thereby rectified. You abolished levies without legitimate grounds, halted nonessential construction and manufacture, and reformed the extravagant and presumptuous…

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
陋習放淫哇之邪聲利無不興弊無不去蓋於
聖祖之良法遵用之也無遺而於
聖祖之美意奉承之也無間是以萬方之大兆民之衆衣
食足而驩然於仰事俯育之天禮義興而勃然於改
過遷善之地四序調於上萬物和於下雋賢熙職戎
夷嚮風此豈無自而然哉良由
陛下之所以富教斯民者不徒崇富教之具而又端一身
以為富教之本故也然天下之大人君不能以獨治
必有分其任者邇年以來為
陛下分富民之任者非無其人也而求其催科弗急加意
===
於民情之休戚者其人鮮矣為
陛下分教民之任者非無其人也而求其化導不倦究心
乎民俗之淳漓者其人亦鮮矣夫為
陛下富民者既非其人則雖無水旱河决之患而民之流
移失業者猶或有之况復罹此患邪然則何怪乎閭
巷之間不能無凍餒田野之内未免於無聊哉夫為
陛下教民者既非其人則雖無凍餒無聊之困而民之作
奸犯科者猶或有之况復值茲困邪然則何怪乎勸
諭切而循理者少赦宥頻而犯法者甚哉蓋饑寒切
身則行甘禽獸利欲汨志則命同螻蟻凡民之情大

身則行甘禽獸利欲汩志則命同螻蟻凡民之情大
punctuated:
陋習，放淫哇之邪聲，利無不興，弊無不去。蓋於聖祖之良法，遵用之也無遺；而於聖祖之美意，奉承之也無間。是以萬方之大、兆民之衆，衣食足而驩然於仰事俯育之天，禮義興而勃然於改過遷善之地。四序調於上，萬物和於下，雋賢熙職，戎夷嚮風，此豈無自而然哉？良由陛下之所以富教斯民者，不徒崇富教之具，而又端一身以為富教之本故也。
然天下之大，人君不能以獨治，必有分其任者。邇年以來，為陛下分富民之任者，非無其人也，而求其催科弗急、加意於民情之休戚者，其人鮮矣。為陛下分教民之任者，非無其人也，而求其化導不倦、究心乎民俗之淳漓者，其人亦鮮矣。
夫為陛下富民者既非其人，則雖無水旱河决之患，而民之流移失業者猶或有之，况復罹此患邪？然則何怪乎閭巷之間不能無凍餒，田野之内未免於無聊哉？夫為陛下教民者既非其人，則雖無凍餒無聊之困，而民之作奸犯科者猶或有之，况復值茲困邪？然則何怪乎勸諭切而循理者少，赦宥頻而犯法者甚哉？蓋饑寒切身，則行甘禽獸；利欲汨志，則命同螻蟻。凡民之情，大
translation_en:
…base customs, and banished licentious and depraved music. Every beneficial measure has been promoted, and every abuse removed. Thus none of the sagely founder’s sound laws has been left unapplied, and his excellent intentions have been upheld without interruption. Throughout the vast realm, the multitude of the people have sufficient clothing and food and rejoice under a Heaven that enables them to support their parents and nurture their children. Ritual propriety and righteousness flourish, and the people eagerly correct their faults and turn toward goodness. The four seasons proceed regularly above, and all things are harmonious below. Talented and worthy men perform their duties splendidly, and the Rong and Yi peoples turn toward your civilizing influence. Could this have come about without a cause? It is indeed because Your Majesty, in enriching and educating the people, does more than promote the means of enriching and educating them: you also make your own person upright as the foundation of that work.
Yet the realm is so vast that its ruler cannot govern it alone; there must be others who share his responsibilities. In recent years, there have certainly been men charged with sharing Your Majesty’s responsibility for enriching the people. Yet few refrain from pressing urgently for tax payments and attend carefully to the people’s welfare and suffering. There have likewise been men charged with sharing Your Majesty’s responsibility for educating the people. Yet few are tireless in transforming and guiding them and devote their attention to whether popular customs are sound or debased.
If those who enrich the people on Your Majesty’s behalf are not the right men, then even without the calamities of floods, droughts, and breaches of river embankments, some people may still wander from their homes and lose their livelihoods. How much more so when they suffer these calamities as well! Why, then, be surprised that cold and hunger persist in the lanes and alleys, and that people in the countryside cannot escape destitution? If those who educate the people on Your Majesty’s behalf are not the right men, then even without the hardships of cold, hunger, and destitution, some people may still commit crimes and violate the law. How much more so when they encounter these hardships as well! Why, then, be surprised that, despite earnest exhortations, few follow moral principle, and that, despite frequent pardons, violations of the law grow more serious? When hunger and cold press upon them, people willingly behave like beasts; when desire for gain overwhelms their resolve, they hold their lives as cheap as those of mole crickets and ants. As for the disposition of the common people, generally …

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
見於
聖策之所先及者臣既述其事論其理如此竊窺
聖策至終篇見
陛下遠想古之帝王富天下有術而教天下有方思舉行
之以繼其治功之盛且於庶富教之三事責臣等悉
心以陳其詳臣之所欲言者上之所陳已露悃幅敢
復申其說於
清問之下
陛下幸無厭焉盖古之御天下者既庶必思所以富之而
制田里薄賦斂則其富之之術也既富必思所以教
===
之而設學校明禮義則其教之之方也富之之術教
之之方布在方策而後世之所以治不古若豈獨富
之者無術而教之者無方之過哉顧為治不能無法
而用法不可無人苟非有文武之君文武之臣决不
能舉文武之政臣故僭言今日之患凡於
陛下承富教之託者宜任其咎而又不量淺深妄勸
陛下以其責臣下者反之以自責也至若庶矣而富富矣
而教此孔子所以告冉有者見於論語其說甚明而
孟軻勸齊梁之君行王者之政亦不過欲其乗地辟
民聚之勢而養以農桑繼以庠序初無異於孔氏之

punctuated:
見於聖策之所先及者，臣既述其事、論其理如此。竊窺聖策至終篇，見陛下遠想古之帝王富天下有術，而教天下有方，思舉行之，以繼其治功之盛，且於庶、富、教之三事，責臣等悉心以陳其詳。臣之所欲言者，上之所陳已露悃幅，敢復申其說於清問之下，陛下幸無厭焉。
盖古之御天下者，既庶，必思所以富之，而制田里、薄賦斂，則其富之之術也；既富，必思所以教之，而設學校、明禮義，則其教之之方也。富之之術、教之之方，布在方策，而後世之所以治不古若，豈獨富之者無術，而教之者無方之過哉？顧為治不能無法，而用法不可無人。苟非有文武之君、文武之臣，决不能舉文武之政。臣故僭言今日之患，凡於陛下承富教之託者，宜任其咎，而又不量淺深，妄勸陛下以其責臣下者，反之以自責也。
至若庶矣而富，富矣而教，此孔子所以告冉有者，見於《論語》，其說甚明。而孟軻勸齊梁之君行王者之政，亦不過欲其乗地辟民聚之勢，而養以農桑，繼以庠序，初無異於孔氏之
translation_en:
…As for what appears among the matters addressed first in Your Majesty’s imperial policy question, your servant has thus recounted the circumstances and discussed their principles. Humbly reading the imperial policy question through to its conclusion, I see that Your Majesty looks far back to the emperors and kings of antiquity, who possessed methods for enriching all under Heaven and means of educating them. You wish to put these into practice, continuing their magnificent achievements in government. Moreover, concerning the three matters of making the population numerous, prosperous, and educated, you charge us, your servants, to devote our utmost attention to setting forth the details. What your servant wishes to say has already been expressed with heartfelt sincerity [?] in the preceding discussion. I venture to elaborate upon it once more in response to your august inquiry, hoping that Your Majesty will not find it tiresome.
Those who governed all under Heaven in antiquity, once the population was numerous, invariably considered how to enrich it. Regulating fields and residential plots and lightening taxes and levies were their methods of enriching the people. Once the people were prosperous, they invariably considered how to educate them. Establishing schools and elucidating ritual propriety and righteousness were their means of educating the people. These methods of enrichment and means of education are set out in the written records. Can the failure of government in later ages to equal that of antiquity be blamed solely on those charged with enriching the people having no methods, and those charged with educating them having no means? Government certainly cannot dispense with institutions, but implementing institutions requires the right people. Without a ruler like Kings Wen and Wu and ministers like theirs, it is decidedly impossible to implement the government of Wen and Wu. Your servant therefore ventures to say that, for the troubles of the present day, all those entrusted by Your Majesty with enriching and educating the people should bear the blame. Yet, without measuring the limits of my understanding, I also rashly urge Your Majesty to turn the reproaches directed at your ministers back upon yourself in self-reproach.
As for enriching the people once they are numerous, and educating them once they are prosperous, this is what Kongzi told Ran You. It appears in the Analects, where the explanation is very clear. When Meng Ke urged the rulers of Qi and Liang to practice kingly government, he likewise wished only that they would take advantage of the expansion of cultivated land and the gathering of the population, sustaining the people through farming and sericulture and following this with schools. This differed in no way from Kongzi’s…

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
說然得道者多助而政刑之效終不若德禮之深德
教之行必始於巨室之慕亦孔孟之遺論也故以先
後言之則庶先乎富富先乎教而君身尤甚所先以
本末言之則教本於富富本於庶而君身為本之大
身也者萬事之根柢萬化之權輿古之聖賢出處異
時窮達異地未嘗不慎重於斯而治之汲汲也故庶
人微矣為庶人者且不可以不修身而况履帝位之
尊一家近矣正一家者且不可以不修身而况治天
下之大苟所求於人者重而所以自任者輕則君子
病之
===
陛下以至儉崇養德之基以至仁立修道之本動靜存誠
蚤夜居敬其於正身以為天下倡者盖不可以有加
矣而臣所以效忠
陛下者於此猶諄諄焉此固臣子望
君無已之心也臣不敢臆說請舉已然之跡徵之粤稽諸
古教民稼穡則稷為之敬敷五教則契為之夏之籲
俊尊帝商之敷求哲人文王用五人而有夏修和武
王臣十人而萬姓悅服帝王之富教天下不獨恃乎
已而必資乎人盖如此然堯則俊德之克明舜則重
華之協帝禹絕旨酒而拜昌言湯躋聖敬以懋厥德

已而必資乎人蓋如此然堯則俊德之克明舜則重
華之協帝禹絕旨酒而拜昌言湯躋聖敬以懋厥德
punctuated:
說。然得道者多助，而政刑之效終不若德禮之深。德教之行，必始於巨室之慕，亦孔孟之遺論也。故以先後言之，則庶先乎富，富先乎教，而君身尤甚所先；以本末言之，則教本於富，富本於庶，而君身為本之大。身也者，萬事之根柢，萬化之權輿。古之聖賢，出處異時，窮達異地，未嘗不慎重於斯，而治之汲汲也。故庶人微矣，為庶人者且不可以不修身，而况履帝位之尊；一家近矣，正一家者且不可以不修身，而况治天下之大。苟所求於人者重，而所以自任者輕，則君子病之。
陛下以至儉崇養德之基，以至仁立修道之本，動靜存誠，蚤夜居敬，其於正身以為天下倡者，盖不可以有加矣。而臣所以效忠陛下者，於此猶諄諄焉，此固臣子望君無已之心也。臣不敢臆說，請舉已然之跡徵之。粤稽諸古，教民稼穡，則稷為之；敬敷五教，則契為之。夏之籲俊尊帝，商之敷求哲人，文王用五人而有夏修和，武王臣十人而萬姓悅服，帝王之富教天下，不獨恃乎已，而必資乎人，盖如此。然堯則俊德之克明，舜則重華之協帝，禹絕旨酒而拜昌言，湯躋聖敬以懋厥德。
translation_en:
…teaching. Yet those who possess the Way receive abundant assistance, and the effects of government and punishments are ultimately less profound than those of virtue and ritual propriety. That the practice of moral instruction must begin with the admiration of the great families is likewise a teaching handed down by Confucius and Meng Ke. Thus, in terms of sequence, a numerous population precedes prosperity, and prosperity precedes instruction; but the ruler’s own person takes precedence above all. In terms of root and branch, instruction is rooted in prosperity, and prosperity in a numerous population; but the ruler’s own person is the greatest root. The person is the foundation of all affairs and the beginning of all transformation. The sages and worthies of antiquity differed in when they served or withdrew and in the circumstances of their obscurity or advancement, yet they invariably treated this matter with care and gravity and diligently attended to its cultivation. Thus, although commoners are humble, even a commoner cannot dispense with self-cultivation—how much more one who occupies the exalted imperial throne! Although a single household lies close at hand, even one who sets a household in order cannot dispense with self-cultivation—how much more one who governs the vast realm! If one demands much of others but assumes little responsibility oneself, the gentleman regards this as a failing.
Your Majesty, through utmost frugality, strengthens the foundation for nurturing virtue and, through utmost benevolence, establishes the basis for cultivating the Way. In activity and repose you preserve sincerity; morning and night you maintain reverence. Your rectification of your own person as an example to the realm surely admits of no improvement. Yet in offering my loyalty to Your Majesty, I continue to urge this earnestly: this is indeed the unceasing hope that a subject cherishes for his ruler. I dare not advance conjectures; allow me to adduce past deeds as evidence. Looking back into antiquity, it was Ji who taught the people to sow and reap, and Xie who reverently disseminated the five teachings. The Xia summoned men of outstanding ability to honor the Lord on High; the Shang sought wise men far and wide. King Wen employed five men, and the Chinese realm was ordered and harmonious; King Wu had ten ministers, and the myriad families gladly submitted. Such was the way emperors and kings enriched and instructed the realm: they did not rely solely upon themselves [?], but necessarily drew upon others. Yet Yao was able to make his eminent virtue shine forth; Shun’s renewed splendor accorded with that of the emperor before him; Yu renounced fine wine and bowed upon hearing excellent counsel; and Tang advanced in sagely reverence, assiduously cultivating his virtue…

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
闡丕顯之謨者柔恭保民兼有丕承之烈者聰明作后
帝王之富教天下不獨資乎人而必本諸身又如此
我
太祖高皇帝肇造鴻業久享天位所以立法貽謀為億萬
載無疆之休者其盡善盡美不異古帝王所以富教
天下之道而周密過之
陛下嗣守丕圖于兹六載
憂民肔切
降詔丁寧治之所期必欲追隆古帝王之盛而不滿乎
漢文帝之為大哉
===
皇言偉哉
聖志臣知
陛下必能踐斯言於無負酬此志於不違而有以弘莫大
之業也然不致力於本之所當先而徒盡心於末之
所可後亦何由滿
陛下之願哉故今日之務固多不可已者而在
陛下所安則自修身之外皆可緩議而徐圖之必也精擇
善利勇决取舍超然遠覽深惟至計信違拂之為恭
思儆戒之可樂兢兢如堯業業如舜克艱如禹待旦
如湯亦臨亦保如文不泄不忘如武屏玩好而親經

punctuated:
闡丕顯之謨者，柔恭保民；兼有丕承之烈者，聰明作后。帝王之富教天下，不獨資乎人，而必本諸身，又如此。

我太祖高皇帝肇造鴻業，久享天位，所以立法貽謀，為億萬載無疆之休者，其盡善盡美，不異古帝王所以富教天下之道，而周密過之。

陛下嗣守丕圖，于兹六載，憂民肔切，降詔丁寧。治之所期，必欲追隆古帝王之盛，而不滿乎漢文帝之為。大哉，皇言！偉哉，聖志！臣知陛下必能踐斯言於無負，酬此志於不違，而有以弘莫大之業也。然不致力於本之所當先，而徒盡心於末之所可後，亦何由滿陛下之願哉？故今日之務，固多不可已者，而在陛下所安，則自修身之外，皆可緩議而徐圖之。必也精擇善利，勇决取舍，超然遠覽，深惟至計，信違拂之為恭，思儆戒之可樂，兢兢如堯，業業如舜，克艱如禹，待旦如湯，亦臨亦保如文，不泄不忘如武，屏玩好而親經
translation_en:
…He who unfolded the greatly illustrious plans was gentle and reverent and protected the people; he who also possessed the achievement of grandly continuing the inheritance was intelligent and discerning as ruler. Thus, too, in enriching and educating all under Heaven, emperors and kings did not rely solely upon others: they necessarily took their own persons as the foundation.

Our Emperor Taizu Gao established the great enterprise and long occupied the heavenly throne. The laws he established and the plans he bequeathed, securing boundless blessings for countless ages, were supremely good and perfect. They matched the ancient emperors’ and kings’ way of enriching and educating all under Heaven, and surpassed it in thoroughness.

Your Majesty has inherited and preserved the great enterprise for six years now. Your concern for the people is earnest [?], and the edict you have issued is full of solemn exhortation. In the government you seek to achieve, you surely desire to recover the flourishing greatness of the ancient emperors and kings, without resting content with the accomplishments of Emperor Wen of Han. How magnificent are the imperial words! How lofty is the imperial resolve! Your servant knows that Your Majesty will surely fulfill these words without falling short and realize this resolve without departing from it, thereby extending this supremely great enterprise. Yet if you do not devote your efforts to the root, which should come first, and instead expend your care only upon the branches, which may come later, how can Your Majesty’s wishes be fulfilled? Among today’s affairs there are indeed many that cannot be abandoned. Yet as regards that upon which Your Majesty rests [?], everything apart from cultivating your own person may be deliberated at leisure and pursued gradually. You must distinguish precisely between goodness and profit, decide resolutely what to embrace and what to reject, rise above immediate concerns to take the long view, and ponder deeply the most far-reaching plans. Recognize that opposition to your wishes can constitute respect, and consider how warnings and admonitions may be welcomed. Be watchful like Yao, vigilant like Shun, diligent in confronting difficulties like Yu, and await the dawn like Tang. Oversee and protect like King Wen; neither slacken nor forget like King Wu. Put aside objects of amusement and draw close to the Classics…

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
史遠邪佞而邇端直畏天之命悉下之情審時之宜
定
國之是凡
聖祖之所以作于前而傳於後者講求其意之宏深推致
利之廣博志焉思繼事焉思述率由舊章之詩不
忘乎心鑒于成憲之書常在乎目操持把握不一時
而少縱不一事而少差如
陛下涖祚之初而愈益勤勵愈益儉約愈益謙恭則一念
慮無非正心一云為無非善道將見推無不準動無
不化公卿勵其職於
===
朝守令勵其職於郡縣四海之内如風行草偃莫不順
從凡
陛下之所憂於天下者不治而自治矣古人有言遵先王
之法而過者未之有也臣既以古人之成效可以為
法於後世者略陳於前又言堯舜之知而不徧物急
先務也臣又以今日之急務在於
陛下之一身者懇陳于後惓惓愚衷不外乎此惟在
陛下俯聽而用之耳盖人主開求言之路必將有聽言之
實人臣遇得言之秋不可無獻言之誠昔之愛君者
其言若此臣嘗誦之以自警今幸遇其秋於用言之

史遠罪佞而邇端貞畏天之命悉下之情審時之宜
定
國之是凡
聖祖之所以作于前而傳於後者講求其意之宏深推致
利之廣博志焉思繼事焉思述率由舊章之詩不
忘乎心鑒于成憲之書常在乎目操持把握不一時
而少縱不一事而少差如
陛下蒞阼之初而愈益勤勵愈益儉約愈益謙恭則一念
慮無非正心一云爲無非善道將見推無不準動無
不化公卿勵其職於
===
朝守令勵其職於郡縣四海之內如風行草偃莫不順
從凡
陛下之所憂於天下者不治而自治矣古人有言遵先王
之法而過者未之有也〔臣〕既以古人之成效可以爲
法於後世者略陳於前又言堯舜之知而不徧物急
先務也〔臣〕又以今日之急務在於
陛下之一身者懇陳于後惓惓愚衷不外乎此惟在
陛下俯聽而用之耳蓋人主開求言之路必將有聽言之
實人臣遇得言之秋不可無獻言之誠昔之愛君者
其言若此〔臣〕嘗誦之以自警今幸遇其秋於用言之
punctuated:
史，遠邪佞而邇端直，畏天之命，悉下之情，審時之宜，定國之是。凡聖祖之所以作于前而傳於後者，講求其意之宏深，推致利之廣博。志焉思繼，事焉思述。《詩》「率由舊章」，不忘乎心；《書》「鑒于成憲」，常在乎目。操持把握，不一時而少縱，不一事而少差。如陛下涖祚之初，而愈益勤勵，愈益儉約，愈益謙恭，則一念慮無非正心，一云為無非善道。將見推無不準，動無不化，公卿勵其職於朝，守令勵其職於郡縣，四海之内，如風行草偃，莫不順從。凡陛下之所憂於天下者，不治而自治矣。
古人有言：「遵先王之法而過者，未之有也。」臣既以古人之成效可以為法於後世者略陳於前，又言：「堯舜之知而不徧物，急先務也。」臣又以今日之急務在於陛下之一身者懇陳于後。惓惓愚衷，不外乎此，惟在陛下俯聽而用之耳。盖人主開求言之路，必將有聽言之實；人臣遇得言之秋，不可無獻言之誠。昔之愛君者，其言若此。臣嘗誦之以自警，今幸遇其秋於用言之
translation_en:
…histories; keep wicked flatterers at a distance and draw upright men near; stand in awe of Heaven’s mandate, understand the circumstances of those below, judge what the times require, and establish what is right for the state. In all that the sagely ancestor instituted before and transmitted to later generations, investigate the breadth and depth of his intentions and extend the wide-reaching benefits. Think of carrying on his aspirations and continuing his undertakings. Never forget in your heart the injunction in the Book of Odes to “follow the old statutes”; keep constantly before your eyes the injunction in the Book of Documents to “take established ordinances as your mirror.” Hold firmly to these principles, allowing no moment of relaxation and no deviation in any matter. Be as you were when Your Majesty first ascended the throne, becoming ever more diligent, frugal, and humble. Then every thought will accord with an upright heart, and every word and action with the way of goodness. We shall see that everything you extend to others accords with the proper standard, and every action brings moral transformation. Dukes and ministers will diligently discharge their duties at court, and prefects and magistrates theirs in the prefectures and counties. Throughout the realm, all will comply, like grass bending before the wind. All the affairs of the realm that trouble Your Majesty will thus come into order of themselves, without further intervention.
An ancient said: “There has never been anyone who followed the laws of the former kings and went astray.” Your servant has already briefly set forth above those proven achievements of the ancients that can serve as models for later generations. Another saying runs: “Even the wisdom of Yao and Shun did not encompass every matter; they gave priority to urgent duties.” Your servant has therefore earnestly explained below that today’s urgent task lies in Your Majesty’s own person. My humble, devoted concern extends no further than this; it remains only for Your Majesty graciously to hear and act upon it. When a ruler opens channels for seeking counsel, he must actually heed that counsel; when a subject encounters an opportunity to speak, he must offer his advice sincerely. Such were the words of those in former times who loved their rulers. Your servant has often recited them as an admonition to himself. Now, fortunately, I have encountered such an opportunity at a court that acts upon counsel…

臣之慶幸哉臣干冒
天威無任戰慄隕越之至臣謹對

主是負所志於平日也故雖言無可采不敢不盡然
睿覽之下倘以其得千慮之一而不忍棄焉則豈特愚
臣之慶幸哉臣干昌
天威無任戰慄殞越之至臣謹對
punctuated: 朝，而不獻其誠於聽言之主，是負所志於平日也。故雖言無可采，不敢不盡。然睿覽之下，倘以其得千慮之一而不忍棄焉，則豈特愚臣之慶幸哉！臣干冒天威，無任戰慄隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …at a court that puts counsel into practice, if I failed to offer my sincere thoughts to a ruler who listens to counsel, I would betray the aspirations I have long cherished. Thus, although my words may contain nothing worth adopting, I dare not withhold any of them. Yet should Your Majesty, upon examining them, judge that among a thousand reflections there is one sound thought and therefore be unwilling to discard them, would it be merely your foolish servant who had cause to rejoice? In presuming to offend Your Majesty’s heavenly authority, I am overcome with trembling and dread, as though about to fall. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
臣徐穆
臣對臣聞帝王之御天下有為政之大要有為政之
大本盖庶也富也教也為政之大要也心也者為政
之大本也富民而不本諸心則無以著其賙恤保愛
之實教民而不本諸心則無以妙其轉移感動之機
是為政不可不務大要務大要不可不端大本大本
既端則推之以富民而民生以遂不待家賜人益自
然田野相安而無凍餒無聊之嘆比閭相保而無流
移失業之人推之以教民而民性以復不待耳提面
命自然遵義遵路而皇極之是歸興仁興讓而澆風
===
===
之不作孰謂存心於富民而不臻其實效存心於教
民而不収其成功也哉是知為政之大要不出於庶
富教三者之外而為政之大本端在於人君一心無
疑矣此心此政之克盡隆古之治所以極於全盛此
心此政之未純漢文之治所以僅為小康然則
今日欲追隆古帝王之盛而陋漢文帝於不居者庸有
出於此心此政之外哉恭惟
皇帝陛下膺天眷之隆荷天責之重巍巍蕩蕩邁唐堯之
峻德戰戰栗栗過周文之小心誕育多方于今六載
即位以来

punctuated:
臣徐穆。
臣對：臣聞帝王之御天下，有為政之大要，有為政之大本。盖庶也、富也、教也，為政之大要也；心也者，為政之大本也。富民而不本諸心，則無以著其賙恤保愛之實；教民而不本諸心，則無以妙其轉移感動之機。是為政不可不務大要，務大要不可不端大本。大本既端，則推之以富民，而民生以遂，不待家賜人益，自然田野相安，而無凍餒無聊之嘆；比閭相保，而無流移失業之人。推之以教民，而民性以復，不待耳提面命，自然遵義遵路，而皇極之是歸；興仁興讓，而澆風之不作。孰謂存心於富民而不臻其實效，存心於教民而不収其成功也哉？是知為政之大要不出於庶、富、教三者之外，而為政之大本端在於人君一心，無疑矣。此心此政之克盡，隆古之治所以極於全盛；此心此政之未純，漢文之治所以僅為小康。然則今日欲追隆古帝王之盛，而陋漢文帝於不居者，庸有出於此心此政之外哉？
恭惟皇帝陛下，膺天眷之隆，荷天責之重，巍巍蕩蕩，邁唐堯之峻德；戰戰栗栗，過周文之小心。誕育多方，于今六載。即位以来，
translation_en:
Your servant Xu Mu.
Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings govern all under Heaven, there are great essentials of government and a great foundation of government. Making the people numerous, prosperous, and educated constitutes the great essentials; the heart constitutes the great foundation. If enriching the people is not rooted in the heart, there is no means of giving concrete expression to relief, protection, and loving care. If educating the people is not rooted in the heart, there is no means of making the subtle workings of transformation and moral influence effective. Thus, in governing, one must attend to the great essentials; and to attend to the great essentials, one must rectify the great foundation. Once that foundation is rectified, extending it to enrich the people enables their livelihoods to flourish. Without requiring gifts to every household or benefits to every individual, people in the countryside will naturally live together in peace, with no lamentations over cold, hunger, or destitution; neighbors will protect one another, and no one will wander away or lose their livelihood. Extending it to educate the people restores their original nature. Without requiring instruction delivered into each person's ear and directly to their face, they will naturally follow righteousness and the proper path, turning toward the imperial standard; they will stir one another to benevolence and deference, and corrupt customs will not arise. Who could say that setting one's heart on enriching the people will fail to produce tangible results, or that setting one's heart on educating them will fail to achieve success? From this we know beyond doubt that the great essentials of government extend no further than these three things—making the people numerous, prosperous, and educated—and that the great foundation of government lies precisely in the ruler's own heart. The complete realization of this heart and this government explains why the rule of high antiquity attained its fullest flourishing. Their incomplete purity explains why the rule of Emperor Wen of Han achieved only moderate well-being. Thus, if today one wishes to emulate the flourishing rule of the emperors and kings of high antiquity, regarding Emperor Wen of Han's achievements as too limited to rest content with, could this possibly be accomplished apart from this heart and this government?
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor has received Heaven's abundant favor and bears the weight of Heaven's charge. Lofty and expansive, you surpass the exalted virtue of Yao of Tang; trembling and vigilant, you exceed the circumspection of King Wen of Zhou. You have broadly nurtured the many regions for six years now. Since ascending the throne…

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
躬耕籍田以勸農已有志於富百姓矣
親臨太學以勸士已有志於教百姓矣是以農桑遍野
而衣食自足於民間絃誦成風而禮樂大行於天下
然猶
體道謙冲
游心高遠民已富而猶以為未富民已化而猶以為未
化乃於
萬幾之暇特進臣等于
廷降賜
清問首詢以漢文帝守成殷富之效中及
===
方今天下未盡富未可教之弊末復欲究庶富教三者
先後本末之序且欲求古人之成效
今日之急務臣有以知
陛下是心即文王視民如傷望道未見之盛心也臣雖愚
陋敢不拜手稽首以對揚
休命於萬一乎臣聞惟天惠民惟辟奉天天不能自養
乎民必賴君以養天不能自教乎民必賴君以教有
君人之責者皆當以教養為心也庶矣而不富富矣
而不教則於為政之大要有所虧而為政之大本亦
有所不能盡矣君人之責固如是乎臣請徵諸古為

translation_en:
…You have personally ploughed the imperial ritual field to encourage agriculture, already showing your resolve to enrich the people. You have personally visited the Imperial University to encourage scholars, already showing your resolve to educate the people. Thus fields and mulberry plantations cover the countryside, and the people have sufficient clothing and food; playing the strings and reciting the classics have become customary, and rites and music flourish throughout the realm. Yet, embodying the Way in modest humility and directing your thoughts toward lofty and far-reaching ends, you regard the people as not yet prosperous even though they are prosperous, and as not yet transformed even though they have been transformed. Accordingly, in a respite from your myriad affairs, you have specially summoned us, your servants, to court and graciously bestowed your august questions. First you ask about the results achieved by Emperor Wen of Han in preserving his inherited rule and bringing prosperity; next you address the present shortcomings whereby not all under Heaven are prosperous or ready to be educated; finally you seek to investigate the proper sequence and relative fundamental and subsidiary importance of increasing the population, enriching it, and educating it. You also seek the proven achievements of the ancients and the urgent tasks of today. From this your servant knows that Your Majesty’s heart is the very same noble heart as that of King Wen, who regarded the people as though they were injured and sought the Way as though he had not yet seen it. Foolish and uncultivated though your servant is, how could I fail to bow with clasped hands and knock my head upon the ground, responding to and extolling even a ten-thousandth part of your gracious command?
Your servant has heard that Heaven bestows kindness upon the people, and the sovereign serves Heaven. Heaven cannot itself nourish the people; it must rely upon the ruler to nourish them. Heaven cannot itself educate the people; it must rely upon the ruler to educate them. All who bear the responsibility of ruling people should therefore make their education and nourishment their heartfelt concern. If the population is numerous but not prosperous, or prosperous but not educated, then something is lacking in the great essentials of government, and the great foundation of government likewise cannot be fully realized. Can this indeed be the proper discharge of a ruler’s responsibility? Your servant begs leave to draw evidence from antiquity and, for…

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
陛下陳之唐虞三代之世風氣既開人物漸繁堯舜禹湯
文武數聖人者任君師之責於上施教養之政於下
播時百穀六府孔脩五十而貢七十而助百畝而徹
故當時耕田鑿井含哺鼓腹烝民乃粒兆民允殖其
富之之效可想見矣慎徽五典敬敷五教夏學曰校
商學曰序周學曰庠故當時百姓昭明治隆俗美比
屋可封歸其有極其教之之效可槩舉矣自是而後
鮮有可稱漢之文帝庶幾乎其躬脩玄默清靜無為
移風易俗與民休息以故海內殷富家給人足戶口
滋殖財貨充溢民既富矣由是禮義之盛興風俗之
===
丕變自重犯法渾乎平明之治耻言人過藹然仁厚
之風亦庶乎其可教也然究其所以則以節儉教化
為之本耳觀其敦樸是尚浮靡不事露臺惜百金之
費端表於己者一節儉也帷帳無文繡之飾作則於
家者一節儉也鰥寡困窮之民則議所以振之水旱
疾疫之災則思所以佐之吳王不朝賜以几杖張武
受賂更加賞賜文帝所以致殷富而興禮義者豈無
所自哉若以分田為定制則夏貢商助周徹之法古
今所常行也寧獨漢乎若以除租為實惠則宗廟百
官四夷之費用度有常經也豈能免乎向使文帝外

punctuated: 陛下陳之。唐虞三代之世，風氣既開，人物漸繁，堯舜禹湯文武數聖人者，任君師之責於上，施教養之政於下。播時百穀，六府孔脩，五十而貢，七十而助，百畝而徹。故當時耕田鑿井，含哺鼓腹，烝民乃粒，兆民允殖，其富之之效可想見矣。慎徽五典，敬敷五教，夏學曰校，商學曰序，周學曰庠。故當時百姓昭明，治隆俗美，比屋可封，歸其有極，其教之之效可槩舉矣。自是而後，鮮有可稱，漢之文帝庶幾乎！其躬脩玄默，清靜無為，移風易俗，與民休息，以故海內殷富，家給人足，戶口滋殖，財貨充溢。民既富矣，由是禮義之盛興，風俗之丕變，自重犯法，渾乎平明之治；耻言人過，藹然仁厚之風，亦庶乎其可教也。然究其所以，則以節儉教化為之本耳。觀其敦樸是尚，浮靡不事，露臺惜百金之費，端表於己者，一節儉也；帷帳無文繡之飾，作則於家者，一節儉也。鰥寡困窮之民，則議所以振之；水旱疾疫之災，則思所以佐之。吳王不朝，賜以几杖；張武受賂，更加賞賜。文帝所以致殷富而興禮義者，豈無所自哉？若以分田為定制，則夏貢商助周徹之法，古今所常行也，寧獨漢乎？若以除租為實惠，則宗廟百官四夷之費，用度有常經也，豈能免乎？向使文帝外
translation_en:
…lay this out before Your Majesty. In the age of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, civilization had begun to flourish, and people and material resources gradually multiplied. The sages Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu assumed from above the responsibilities of ruler and teacher, and extended policies of instruction and nourishment to those below. The various grains were sown in their seasons, and the six resources were thoroughly managed. There was the tribute system on fifty mu, the labor-assistance system on seventy mu, and the shared-levy system on a hundred mu. Thus people then tilled their fields and dug their wells, ate their fill and patted their bellies contentedly. The masses had grain to eat, and the myriad people truly prospered. One can readily imagine how effectively these rulers enriched their people. They carefully promoted the five constant relationships and reverently disseminated the five teachings. The schools of the Xia were called xiao, those of the Shang xu, and those of the Zhou xiang. Thus the people were enlightened, government flourished, and customs were good. Every household had someone worthy of receiving a fief, and all turned toward the supreme standard. The effects of their instruction can thus be broadly described.

After this, few rulers deserve commendation. Emperor Wen of the Han came close! He personally cultivated profound quietude, remaining tranquil and refraining from intervention. He transformed customs and allowed the people rest and recovery. Consequently, all within the seas grew prosperous: households had enough and individuals were well supplied; households and population multiplied; and wealth and goods abounded. Once the people were prosperous, ritual propriety and righteousness flourished greatly, and customs underwent a profound transformation. People valued their own standing and [avoided?] breaking the law, producing an all-pervading order of impartiality and clarity. They were ashamed to speak of others’ faults, and a spirit of benevolence and generosity prevailed. They were thus nearly ready to receive instruction as well. Yet, when we examine how this came about, its foundation was simply frugality and moral instruction.

Consider how he esteemed simplicity and had no dealings with extravagance. He begrudged spending a hundred units of gold on a terrace: in setting an upright example through his own conduct, he practiced frugality throughout. His curtains and hangings had no patterned embroidery: in establishing a model within his household, he likewise practiced frugality throughout. For widowers, widows, and people in poverty and distress, he deliberated on ways to provide relief. When floods, droughts, disease, or epidemics struck, he considered how to assist those affected. When the Prince of Wu failed to attend court, he bestowed an armrest and staff upon him. When Zhang Wu accepted bribes, he granted him still more rewards. Surely Emperor Wen’s success in bringing prosperity and fostering ritual propriety and righteousness had its source!

If the allocation of fields is regarded as an established system, then the Xia tribute system, the Shang labor-assistance system, and the Zhou shared-levy system were methods regularly practiced in antiquity and later times. Were they peculiar to the Han? If the remission of land tax is regarded as a tangible benefit, the expenses of the ancestral temples, the officials, and relations with the peoples of the four quarters nevertheless followed regular requirements. How could these be dispensed with? Had Emperor Wen outwardly…

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
施教養之政内無教養之心雖求索極於錙銖而無
常之賜用如泥沙征歛至於毛髮而不急之需棄若
土芥化導雖明而冥頑者自若懷柔雖切而武斷者
益驕如武帝之海内虚耗戶口減半法網嚴密盗賊
繁興者所必至矣尚何殷富刑措之足言乎此臣愚
斷斷然以為文帝殷富之效禮義之興盖根本於節
儉教化之所致也洪惟我
太祖高皇帝天縱聖神肇造區夏薄海内外罔不臣服其
富民也畫田連夫阡陌而兼併有刑遊惰有禁其教
民也設學遍於郡縣而立教有條司教有官

translation_en:
…outwardly implemented policies to educate and nourish the people, yet inwardly lacked the intention to do so, then even if he exacted the smallest amounts, his irregular gifts would have squandered resources like mud and sand; even if his levies reached down to a hair’s breadth, expenditure on nonessential needs would have cast resources away like dirt and weeds. Though his moral guidance was clear, the obstinately ignorant would have remained unchanged; though his efforts at conciliation were earnest, those who ruled by force would have grown more arrogant. Conditions like those under Emperor Wu—depletion throughout the realm, the halving of households and population, a tight net of laws, and proliferating banditry—would inevitably have followed. How, then, could one speak of prosperity and punishments left unused? This is why I, your ignorant servant, firmly believe that the prosperity achieved under Emperor Wen and the flourishing of ritual propriety and righteousness were fundamentally brought about by frugality and moral instruction.
I reverently consider that our Emperor Taizu Gao, endowed by Heaven with sagely and divine qualities, founded his dominion over the Chinese realm; throughout the lands within and beyond the seas, none failed to submit as his subjects. To enrich the people, he demarcated fields and linked cultivators along the field paths [?], established punishments for the engrossment of land, and prohibited idleness. To educate the people, he established schools throughout the prefectures and counties, with regulations governing instruction and officials charged with overseeing it. Successive sage emperors further enhanced their continuation of his work. Thus, throughout this vast realm, farmers applied themselves to cultivation without fear of failing to prosper, and scholars applied themselves to learning without concern that they would prove difficult to transform. More than 120 years have now elapsed; the population has grown ever more numerous and the territory ever more extensive. In great commercial centers and large cities, marketplaces stand within sight of one another; in remote corners and distant borderlands, chickens and dogs can be heard from one settlement to the next. Even in the fullest flourishing of high antiquity, the population never exceeded that of today.
Yet as laws endure, people gradually grow careless of them; as an age continues, customs gradually decline. Arrogance, extravagance, ostentation, and the usurpation of privileges spread through mutual imitation, becoming common practice, while the people whom our imperial ancestors had enriched grow daily more exhausted and impoverished. Unrestrained, perverse, depraved, and extravagant conduct knows no bounds, while the people whom our imperial ancestors had morally transformed grow daily more shallow and insincere. At this time of utmost flourishing, such things surely ought not to exist. Hence Your Majesty cannot but be concerned to emulate Emperor Wen of Han in preserving an inherited achievement. Yet your servant has heard that Ran You said: “Now that the people are numerous, what further…”

加焉孔子曰富之
方今天下之人務本者少逐末者多勤身者少遊手者
多平居暇日不浮費於道佛之奉則虛縻於衣食之
資小夫窶人所入不足以供其所出富家巨室所積
不足以補其所需是以頃因水旱輒流移以他徙繼
遭河决復轉盼而别居閭閻之内人不聊生田野之
間坐而待斃民之不富誠有如
聖問之所慮者為今之計莫若弘儉約之風擇撫字之職
嚴上下之分定僭踰之罪異端足以蠹民財者則斥
絕之淫巧足以耗民財者則痛革之如是則有財者
===
不得以濫用無財者不得以強用庶乎民有餘財而
可富也富民之政雖出於
上然非有仁心以為之本則亦徒為文具而非真心實惠
之形矣臣願

之功恐有以傷民財我則息之欲信禱祠之事恐有

translation_en:
…should further be done for them?” Confucius said, “Enrich them.”
Among the people of the realm today, few pursue the fundamental occupation of agriculture, while many pursue subsidiary occupations; few labor diligently, while many remain idle. In their everyday leisure, if they do not squander money on Daoist and Buddhist observances, they waste it on clothing and food. The earnings of humble, impoverished people cannot cover their expenditures; the accumulated wealth of rich families and great households cannot meet their wants. Thus, when floods and droughts recently occurred, people promptly scattered and migrated elsewhere; when river embankments subsequently burst, they again changed their dwelling places in the blink of an eye. In the villages, people cannot sustain their livelihoods; in the fields, they sit awaiting death. The people's lack of prosperity is indeed as Your Majesty's sagely question apprehends. For the present, no policy would be better than to promote frugality, select suitable men for offices charged with nurturing the people, enforce distinctions between superior and inferior, and establish penalties for overstepping one's station. Heterodox teachings that drain the people's wealth should be rejected and eliminated; extravagant craftsmanship that consumes their wealth should be thoroughly abolished. In this way, those with wealth would not be permitted to spend it recklessly, and those without wealth would not be permitted to spend beyond their means. Then perhaps the people would have resources to spare and could become prosperous.
Although policies to enrich the people issue from above, unless they rest upon a benevolent heart, they will amount merely to formal paperwork, rather than expressions of sincere concern and tangible benefit. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty, desiring to give greater attention to the people, would first put these principles into practice personally. In every receipt or disbursement of funds, say: “I fear spending recklessly without any substantive purpose.” In every bestowal of an object, say: “I fear granting rewards indiscriminately where there is no merit.” When contemplating construction works, think: “I fear that this may damage the people's resources; I shall therefore suspend it.” When inclined to place faith in prayers and sacrifices, think: “I fear that this may exhaust the people's resources; I shall therefore stop it.” We shall then see the way to prosperity practiced at court and extended throughout the realm. When the gnomon is upright, its shadow will naturally be straight; when the source is clean, its flow will naturally be clear. These people, already numerous, will become prosperous of themselves without prosperity having to be deliberately sought. Your servant has also heard that Ran You said: “Once they are prosperous, what further…”

…is to be added?” Confucius said, “Educate them.”

At present, among the people throughout the realm, few possess understanding and many lack it; few follow moral instruction and many resist it. Gathering together all day, if they are not continually transgressing the great bounds of proper conduct [?], they delight in exercising petty cleverness. Common people and young folk act without understanding what they do and grow accustomed to practices without examining them. Students of the Classics and learned scholars fail to choose discerningly or hold firmly to their choices. Thus, although exhortations grow earnest and urgent day after day, they remain benighted and unaware; although pardons and acts of clemency are repeatedly granted, they remain complacent and unrestrained. Those who slip through the net of the law live on, having escaped by good fortune; those who violate the sovereign’s laws die without remorse. The people’s resistance to instruction is indeed as Your Majesty’s sagely question fears. The best course now is to strengthen the foundations of moral education, attach importance to the offices responsible for moral guidance, employ men of simplicity and substantial virtue, and restrain the frivolous and shallow. Where accumulated abuses sap scholars’ morale, revive it; where corrupt customs spoil scholars’ conduct, reform them. In this way, those without goodness will look to models and find encouragement, while those who possess goodness will be moved to still greater effort. Then perhaps all the people will incline toward goodness and become receptive to instruction.

Although policies for educating the people issue from above, unless they are rooted in a benevolent heart, they merely make a fine display; they do not extend what one has personally practiced and inwardly grasped. Your servant wishes that, in seeking to inspire the people, Your Majesty would first put your own conduct in order. When advancing someone to office, ask: “Does this accord with public judgment?” When dismissing someone, ask: “Might this obstruct the employment of talent?” Upright men and principled scholars are effective instruments of the state: draw them close. Petty and treacherous men are great pests preying on the people: keep them at a distance. Then fitting moral guidance will prevail at court and reach throughout the realm. When the basin is round, the water is also round; when the basin is square, the water is also square. Once these people are prosperous, they will transform themselves without needing to be transformed. 則刑辟易犯此相因之勢亦自然之理也夫弊之生
也起於相因則處之之道亦必有相因者存焉故欲
民之不犯夫刑辟必敦夫教化欲敦夫教化必尚夫
禮義欲尚夫禮義必足夫衣食欲足夫衣食必務夫
耕桑誠如是則無不可處之道無不可救之弊無不
可富無不可教之民矣尚何足以勞
聖慮哉抑是相因之道理易知事易行推原其本特在
聖心一運用間耳臣請復徵諸古以畢其說唐虞三代之
君存心於天下加志於窮民民之饑寒則曰我饑寒
===
之民之有罪則曰我陷之也一饋而身至於十起一
沐而髮至於三握德及禽獸化行蠻貊堯舜禹湯文
武教養之心何如哉向使既庶而不繼以富之之術
既富而不繼以教之之方則阻饑者誰教以耕耨艱
食者誰教以佃漁而富民之仁心不於是而泯沒邪
日用不知者誰與開先逸居無教者誰與警悟而教
民之仁心不於是而淪喪邪唐虞三代之君存心於
富民而民遂其生存心於教民而民復其性其於為
政之大要烏有不舉而大本烏有不盡乎成規定制
昭然具在舉而措之則唐虞三代之治復見於

This tendency of one thing to follow from another is also a natural principle. Traced to its root, it depends only upon the exercise of Your Majesty’s sagely mind.

The rulers of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties set their hearts upon all under Heaven and devoted their attention to the impoverished. When the people suffered hunger and cold, they said, “It is I who have made them hungry and cold.” When the people committed crimes, they said, “It is I who have led them into this.” During a single meal they rose as many as ten times; during a single washing of their hair they grasped their hair as many as three times to interrupt the washing. Their virtue reached even birds and beasts, and their transforming influence extended to the Man and Mo peoples. How great was the concern of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu to teach and nourish the people! Had they failed, once the people were numerous, to follow with means of enriching them, or, once they were prosperous, to follow with methods of teaching them, who would have taught those afflicted by hunger to plow and weed, or those struggling for food to hunt and fish? Would not their benevolent concern to enrich the people thereby have vanished? Who would have first enlightened those who acted daily without understanding, or awakened those who lived at ease without instruction? Would not their benevolent concern to teach the people thereby have been lost? translation_en:
…today. What need is there even to speak of the comparatively modest Emperor Wen of Han? I respectfully consider how Your Majesty has inherited and preserves the great enterprise of your ancestors, deliberates upon the way of governing, and wishes to equal the glory of the emperors and kings of high antiquity. Your foolish servant believes that, to equal their glory, one must seek their methods of government; to seek their methods of government, one must seek their heart. As for Emperor Wen of Han, although he carried out the essentials of government, he was content with small achievements; although he fully attended to its great foundation, he did not realize its fullest application. Why, then, need I trouble Your Majesty with a detailed account of him?
As for the order of precedence and the relation of root to branch among the three tasks of increasing the population, enriching it, and educating it, your foolish servant believes that only once the people are numerous can they be enriched. If they are not numerous, the inhabitants are few, and wealth and goods cannot adequately be produced. Only once they are prosperous can they be educated. If they are not prosperous, they lack even the means to save themselves from death and have no leisure to attend to ritual propriety and righteousness. Viewed in this light, their order of precedence must not be confused, nor their relation of root to branch disordered. Yet their great foundation lies solely in Your Majesty’s heart. Once this heart is preserved, the achievements of the ancients can be examined and understood, and the urgent tasks of today can likewise be carried out in due sequence.
These urgent tasks amount simply to such plans for enriching the people as your servant has described. Otherwise, resources will be limited while expenditure is boundless: one person tills the soil, and ten gather to eat what he produces; what is accumulated in ten days is squandered and consumed in one. It would then be difficult to make the people prosperous and well supplied. The Book of Changes says, “Practice restraint through institutions and regulations, without injuring wealth or harming the people.” This is what it means. These tasks likewise amount simply to such plans for educating the people as your servant has described. Otherwise, although people outwardly comply, their hearts remain unchanged. One person from Qi instructs someone, while a crowd from Chu clamors around him; give something one day of warmth, then subject it to ten days of cold. Your servant has already briefly set forth his views in response to Your Majesty’s sagely questions, but at the close of this essay he has a further offering to make.

The mind is difficult to hold fast and easy to let go; government is difficult to set in motion and easy to let lapse. When this mind is preserved, the great foundation is established: all the eight farthest regions lie clearly within my gates, and everything within the Four Seas falls within my consideration. There is then no affair of government under Heaven that cannot be accomplished. When this mind is not preserved, the great foundation is lost: selfishness marks out boundaries within the tiny space of the heart, and whatever lies beyond a single membrane becomes as alien as Hu and Yue. It must be held fast and preserved, examined and scrutinized, and must not be abandoned even for an instant. Yet it comes and goes at no fixed time, and no one knows its whereabouts. When it gathers within one’s breast, others cannot know it; only oneself knows it. When it roams a thousand li away, others cannot know it; only oneself knows it.

臣羅欽順。
臣對：臣聞人君所以致天下之大治而成天下之大化者，亦惟全天德以行乎王道而已。萬邦咸寧，天下之大治也；黎民於變，天下之大化也。心正身脩，德之純乎天也；用賢立政，道之純乎王也。致治成化而非道，則綱維不張而精神徒弊；行道而非德，則奮迅未幾而委靡已形。故有志於帝王之治，不可不求其道；有志於帝王之道，不可不求其德。誠使方寸之天不雜，本原之地惟清，必能立經陳紀，用罔丕基，翕受敷施，爰煕庶績。以之富民，自有以遂其飽暖之願；以之教民，自有以興其禮義之風。治化浹於敷天，而聲聞流於率土矣。二帝三王之所以卓冠百王者，以其全盡乎此也；漢文帝之所以幾致刑措者，以其僅得乎此也。然則今日所以追隆古之盛而陋文帝於不為者，道豈遠乎哉？亦曰致乎天德之全，極乎王道之備耳。
洪惟我太祖高皇帝受天明命，奄有四海，脩德行仁，以養以教，聖謨丕顯，萬世足徵。承以五宗，益隆繼述，生齒之繁、疆域之廣，過前代遠矣。欽惟皇帝陛下以至聖之德嗣大寶之位，恭勤不怠，仁厚有加。
translation_en:
Your servant Luo Qinshun.
Your servant replies: I have heard that the means by which a ruler brings about great order throughout the world and accomplishes its great moral transformation consist solely in perfecting heavenly virtue and thereby practicing the Kingly Way. All the states enjoying peace together constitutes great order throughout the world; the common people becoming transformed constitutes its great moral transformation. Rectifying the mind and cultivating the person make virtue purely accord with Heaven; employing the worthy and establishing government make the Way purely accord with true kingship. If one seeks order and transformation without the Way, the guiding bonds will not be upheld, and one's energies will merely be exhausted. If one practices the Way without virtue, scarcely has vigorous effort begun before lassitude appears. Thus, anyone aspiring to the government of the ancient emperors and kings must seek their Way; anyone aspiring to their Way must seek their virtue. If the heavenly nature within the heart is truly unmixed and its source remains pure, one will surely be able to establish enduring principles and set out governing rules, thereby laying a great foundation [?], receiving all together and dispensing broadly, and thus bringing the many undertakings to flourishing completion. By enriching the people through this, one will naturally fulfill their wish for sufficient food and clothing; by teaching the people through this, one will naturally foster their practice of ritual propriety and righteousness. Order and moral transformation will pervade all beneath Heaven, and their renown will spread throughout the land. The reason the Two Emperors and Three Kings stood preeminent among all rulers was that they fully realized this. The reason Emperor Wen of the Han nearly reached the point at which punishments could be set aside was that he attained even a little of it. If, then, we seek today to match the flourishing age of high antiquity and regard Emperor Wen's achievements as too limited to pursue, can the Way to do so be far away? It is simply to attain the fullness of heavenly virtue and the completeness of the Kingly Way.
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao received Heaven's bright mandate and possessed all within the Four Seas. He cultivated virtue and practiced benevolence, nourishing and teaching the people. His sagely plans shone resplendently and provide a model for ten thousand generations. The five ancestral emperors who succeeded him further enhanced the continuation of his work; the abundance of the population and the extent of the territory far surpassed those of earlier dynasties. We reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor, with the virtue of utmost sageliness, succeeded to the imperial throne. You have been respectful and diligent without flagging, and ever more benevolent and generous …

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
治化之成盖已駸駸乎其日盛矣然猶不自滿假廼
於
萬幾之暇登進臣等于
廷咨以庶富教之道俾陳其本末先後與夫古人之成
效
今日之急務臣伏而讀之有以知
陛下之養民直欲如隆古之咸寧教民直欲如隆古之於
變而後已此天下之幸
宗社之福也臣雖愚陋敢不罄所聞知以對揚
清問之萬一乎臣聞天生斯民立之司牧而寄以三事
===
曰庶曰富曰教是已庶而不富則民無以遂其生富
而不教則民無以復其性是以受天命以君天下者
必富之於既庶之餘教之於既富之後使民生咸遂
民性咸復然後天人之望允塞而君師之責無慚制
田里薄稅斂所以富之也立學校明禮義所以教之
也旁招俊乂布列庶位所以分任教養之責也然人
君一心實萬化之原一身實天下之本惟夫心得其
正而私欲無所容身得其脩而偏僻無所累則善政
之立得以究其功賢人之用得以行其志苟無其本
不免於內外之背馳首尾之乖剌而欲治化之成也

不免於內外之背馳首尾之乖剌而欲治化之成也
punctuated:
治化之成，盖已駸駸乎其日盛矣。然猶不自滿假，廼於萬幾之暇，登進臣等于廷，咨以庶富教之道，俾陳其本末先後，與夫古人之成效、今日之急務。臣伏而讀之，有以知陛下之養民，直欲如隆古之咸寧；教民，直欲如隆古之於變而後已。此天下之幸，宗社之福也。臣雖愚陋，敢不罄所聞知，以對揚清問之萬一乎？
臣聞天生斯民，立之司牧，而寄以三事，曰庶、曰富、曰教，是已。庶而不富，則民無以遂其生；富而不教，則民無以復其性。是以受天命以君天下者，必富之於既庶之餘，教之於既富之後，使民生咸遂，民性咸復，然後天人之望允塞，而君師之責無慚。制田里，薄稅斂，所以富之也；立學校，明禮義，所以教之也；旁招俊乂，布列庶位，所以分任教養之責也。然人君一心，實萬化之原；一身，實天下之本。惟夫心得其正，而私欲無所容；身得其脩，而偏僻無所累，則善政之立，得以究其功；賢人之用，得以行其志。苟無其本，不免於內外之背馳、首尾之乖剌，而欲治化之成也，
translation_en:
…The accomplishments of your governance and moral transformation have surely been advancing swiftly, flourishing more each day. Yet you remain unsatisfied with your achievements. Amid the countless affairs of state, you have found time to summon us, your servants, to court and consult us on how to make the people numerous, prosperous, and educated. You have directed us to set forth the fundamentals and particulars, the proper sequence, the achievements of the ancients, and the urgent tasks of the present day. Reading your question with reverence, I understand that in sustaining the people, Your Majesty will rest only when all enjoy peace, as in high antiquity; in educating them, only when they are morally transformed, as in high antiquity. This is good fortune for all under Heaven and a blessing for the dynastic ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain. Though ignorant and unlearned, dare I fail to exhaust what I have heard and know, in answering and honoring even one ten-thousandth of your august inquiry?
I have heard that Heaven brought forth these people, established rulers to shepherd them, and entrusted those rulers with three tasks: making the people numerous, making them prosperous, and educating them. If the people are numerous but not prosperous, they have no means to sustain their lives fully; if prosperous but uneducated, they have no means to restore their original moral nature. Thus those who receive Heaven’s mandate to rule all under Heaven must enrich the people once they are numerous and educate them once they are prosperous. They must enable every person’s livelihood to flourish and every person’s moral nature to be restored. Only then will the expectations of Heaven and the people truly be fulfilled, and the ruler have no cause for shame in discharging his responsibilities as sovereign and teacher. Regulating fields and residential holdings and lightening taxation are the means of enriching the people. Establishing schools and elucidating ritual propriety and righteousness are the means of educating them. Seeking out outstanding men far and wide and placing them in the various offices are the means of sharing responsibility for educating and sustaining the people. Yet the ruler’s own mind is truly the source of all transformation, and his own person is truly the foundation of all under Heaven. Only when his mind is rectified, leaving no room for selfish desires, and his person cultivated, unburdened by partiality or perversity, can the good policies he establishes achieve their full effect and the worthy men he employs carry out their aspirations. Without this foundation, his inward disposition and outward conduct will inevitably run counter to one another, and beginning and end will be at odds; yet to expect governance and moral transformation to succeed…

text:
豈不難哉故曰徒善不足以為政徒法不能以自行
此之謂也
陛下欲考成效於古人臣請徵諸唐虞三代以對若漢文
帝之事功則非臣之所敢望於
陛下者彼其萬邦咸寧六府孔脩兆民允殖四方和恒唐
虞三代之治何如也黎民於變四方風動厥師用爽
四海永清唐虞三代之化何如也夫治不徒致化不
徒成其富民也則有井田之制有貢助徹之法而任
其責者又有若后稷以播百穀有若伯益以奏艱食
思艱圖易責之於君牙是富之有其道矣其教民也
===
則有學校之設有詩書禮樂之教而任其責者又有
若契以為司徒有若禹以化讒說敬敷在德責之於
君陳是教之有其道矣然而俊德之克明厥身之慎
脩則王道之行於堯舜者夫豈無其本乎厥中之允
執大德之懋昭明德之克慎則王道之行於禹湯文
武者夫豈無其本乎本於內者極其純行於外者極
其至故養民而民遂其生教民而民復其性耕田鑿
井於不識不知之天遵義遵道於蕩蕩平平之域此
唐虞三代之治化所以非後世之所能及也歟自時
厥後鮮有可稱所以富民者雖有代田限田之制有

…would this not be difficult? Thus it is said: “Goodness alone is insufficient for governing; laws alone cannot put themselves into effect.” This is what those words mean.
Your Majesty wishes to examine the achievements of the ancients. Your servant asks leave to answer by drawing evidence from Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. As for the accomplishments of Emperor Wen of Han, your servant would not presume to set these as the standard for Your Majesty. All their myriad states were at peace; the six resources were thoroughly put in order; the multitude of people truly prospered; and the four quarters enjoyed enduring harmony. What government flourished under Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties! The common people were transformed; the four quarters responded as if moved by the wind; the multitudes thereby became enlightened; and all within the four seas enjoyed lasting tranquillity. What moral transformation prevailed under Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties! Good government is not achieved without means, nor does moral transformation come about of itself. To enrich the people, they had the well-field system and the gong, zhu, and che methods of taxation. Among those entrusted with this responsibility were Hou Ji, who sowed the various grains, and Bo Yi, who secured sustenance when food was hard to obtain. To consider difficulties and plan for ease was the responsibility charged to Jun Ya. Thus they had the proper means of enriching the people. To educate the people, they established schools and taught the Odes, Documents, rites, and music. Among those entrusted with this responsibility were Xie, who served as Minister of Education, and Yu, who reformed those who uttered slanders. Reverently spreading instruction founded on virtue was the responsibility charged to Jun Chen. Thus they had the proper means of educating the people. Yet the ability to manifest eminent virtue and carefully cultivate oneself—were these not the foundations of the Kingly Way as practised by Yao and Shun? Truly holding fast to the mean, striving to make great virtue manifest, and carefully attending to illustrious virtue—were these not the foundations of the Kingly Way as practised by Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu? What was rooted within attained utmost purity; what was practised without attained utmost perfection. Thus, when they nourished the people, the people fulfilled their lives; when they educated the people, the people recovered their original nature. They ploughed their fields and dug their wells under a heaven whose workings they neither perceived nor understood, and followed righteousness and the Way in a realm of breadth and evenness. Surely this explains why later ages could not equal the government and moral transformation of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties! From that time onward, there was little worthy of praise. title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
口分世業之法然求其效如古之咸寧不可得矣所
以教民者雖有臨雍拜老之儀有增廣生員之舉然
求其效如古之於變不可得矣所以然者得非王道
有所未備天德有所未全乎求其庶幾焉者僅漢之
文帝一人而已故觀班史之所載曰海內殷富則庶
幾乎富民之效曰興於禮義則庶幾乎教民之效所
以斷獄四百幾致刑措而守成之美彷彿成康要其
所以得此者豈有他哉蓋躬行節儉則有得乎天德
之一端減除田租則有得乎王道之一節故其治化
之成就亦有得乎唐虞三代之彷彿也使其獲聞大
===
學之道而致乎天德之全能求大賢之用而極乎王
道之備抑豪強之兼并興禮樂於久淪則其所至豈
止於此而已哉此臣於文帝之事所以不欲屑屑為
陛下道也而
陛下且疑其田租既除則用度何給臣又不敢不推其所
以焉蓋當文帝之時無冗濫之官無坐食之卒加以
節用固應沛然況田租雖暫除而園林山澤之賦固
在費出有經何憂其不給乎夫古人之成效臣既畢
陳於前矣若夫
今日之急務臣雖不克詳究而

節用固應沛然況田租雖除而園林山澤之賦固
在費出有經何憂其不給乎夫古人之成效臣既畢
陳於前矣若夫
今日之急務臣雖不克詳究而
punctuated:
口分世業之法，然求其效如古之咸寧，不可得矣。所以教民者，雖有臨雍拜老之儀，有增廣生員之舉，然求其效如古之於變，不可得矣。所以然者，得非王道有所未備，天德有所未全乎？求其庶幾焉者，僅漢之文帝一人而已。故觀班史之所載，曰「海內殷富」，則庶幾乎富民之效；曰「興於禮義」，則庶幾乎教民之效。所以斷獄四百，幾致刑措，而守成之美彷彿成康。要其所以得此者，豈有他哉？蓋躬行節儉，則有得乎天德之一端；減除田租，則有得乎王道之一節。故其治化之成就，亦有得乎唐虞三代之彷彿也。使其獲聞大學之道，而致乎天德之全，能求大賢之用，而極乎王道之備，抑豪強之兼并，興禮樂於久淪，則其所至，豈止於此而已哉？此臣於文帝之事，所以不欲屑屑為陛下道也。而陛下且疑其田租既除，則用度何給，臣又不敢不推其所以焉。蓋當文帝之時，無冗濫之官，無坐食之卒，加以節用，固應沛然。況田租雖暫除，而園林山澤之賦固在，費出有經，何憂其不給乎？
夫古人之成效，臣既畢陳於前矣。若夫今日之急務，臣雖不克詳究，而
translation_en:
…and the regulations for individually allotted and hereditary land. Yet results comparable to the universal peace of antiquity could not be attained. As for educating the people, there were ceremonies in which the sovereign visited the imperial academy and paid homage to elders, and measures to increase the number of government students. Yet results comparable to the transformation achieved in antiquity could not be attained. Was this not because the kingly Way remained incomplete and Heavenly virtue had not been fully realized? Among those who came close, there was only Emperor Wen of the Han. Thus, when we examine what is recorded in Ban Gu’s History of the Han, the statement that “all within the seas was prosperous and wealthy” indicates an approximation to the results of enriching the people; the statement that “they were inspired by ritual propriety and righteousness” indicates an approximation to the results of educating them. Consequently, only four hundred criminal cases were adjudicated, punishments came close to being set aside, and the excellence with which he preserved his inherited achievements resembled that of Kings Cheng and Kang. What other explanation could there be for his attaining this? By personally practicing frugality, he grasped one aspect of Heavenly virtue; by reducing and abolishing the land tax, he grasped one element of the kingly Way. Thus, his accomplishments in government and moral transformation also bore some resemblance to those of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties.
Had he been able to hear the Way of the Great Learning and fully realize Heavenly virtue, to secure the service of great worthies and bring the kingly Way to completion, to restrain the powerful from engrossing land, and to revive rites and music after their long decline, would his achievements have stopped at this? This is why your servant has not wished to recount Emperor Wen’s affairs to Your Majesty in minute detail. Yet Your Majesty also questions how expenditure could be met once the land tax had been abolished, and your servant therefore dares not omit an inquiry into the reasons. In Emperor Wen’s time, there were no superfluous or improperly appointed officials, and no soldiers drawing sustenance in idleness. With economy in expenditure as well, resources should certainly have been plentiful. Moreover, although the land tax was temporarily abolished, levies on gardens, groves, mountains, and marshes remained in place. With expenditure subject to established rules, why fear that resources would be insufficient?
Your servant has already fully set forth above the accomplishments of the ancients. As for the urgent tasks of the present day, although your servant has been unable to investigate them in detail, yet…

punctuated:
聖問所及，亦不敢不少效其愚。陛下受六聖撫摩之民，當十紀亨嘉之運，銳情教養，動法祖宗，致令版籍所登遠過漢唐盛際。飽暖之願遂矣，禮義之風興矣。聖策下詢，且猶慮其凍餒之不免，而流移之漸多；循理之尚少，而犯法之愈甚。推其必至之勢，咨以善處之方，此固陛下視民如傷、深自抑畏之盛心也。然天下至大，生民至眾，萬有一焉，或有如陛下之所慮者。陛下必欲普遂羣生，茂隆丕業，則所以處乎此者，誠不可不加之意焉。臣愚竊以為，斯民之輕犯刑辟，陛下既知其由於衣食之不足、禮義之不治矣。足其衣食，驅之禮義，刑其有不措哉？然則欲求所以處乎此者，亦惟盡心於富教焉耳。

臣請以富民之道言之。國家田里之制已有定矣，輕稅斂，減徭役，則今日富民之所當急也。然欲稅斂之輕，在於罷不急之務，杜無功之賞，汰罷惰之卒，裁濫額之官，省無名之費；欲徭役之減，在於息土木之工，卻遠方之貢，嚴驛
translation_en:
…on the matters raised in Your Majesty’s sagely questions, I dare not fail to offer at least my humble thoughts. Your Majesty has inherited a people nurtured by six sage sovereigns and reigns amid the prosperity of ten twelve-year cycles. You devote yourself earnestly to educating and nourishing the people, taking the imperial ancestors as your model in every action. Consequently, the population entered in the registers far surpasses that of the Han and Tang at their height. The people’s wish for adequate food and clothing has been fulfilled, and a spirit of ritual propriety and righteousness has arisen. Yet in sending down your sagely policy question, you still express concern that they cannot escape cold and hunger and that displacement and migration are gradually increasing; that too few follow moral principles and that violations of the law grow ever more serious. You infer where these tendencies must lead and ask how best to address them. This indeed expresses Your Majesty’s noble concern for the people, treating them as though they were injured, and your profound humility and vigilance. Nevertheless, the realm is immense and its people exceedingly numerous: in one case among ten thousand, circumstances may indeed be as Your Majesty fears. If Your Majesty wishes to enable all living people to flourish and greatly advance your grand undertaking, you must give careful attention to the means of addressing this.

In my humble judgment, Your Majesty already knows that the people’s readiness to incur criminal penalties arises from insufficient food and clothing and a failure to cultivate ritual propriety and righteousness. Provide them with adequate food and clothing and guide them toward propriety and righteousness: could punishments then fail to be set aside? Thus, to seek the means of addressing these matters requires only wholehearted devotion to enriching and educating the people.

Allow me to speak of the way to enrich the people. The state’s system governing fields and residential settlements is already established. Lightening taxes and reducing corvée labor are therefore the urgent tasks for enriching the people today. To lighten taxes, however, requires ending nonessential undertakings, preventing rewards for those without merit, discharging indolent soldiers, eliminating supernumerary officials, and reducing expenditures without legitimate purpose. To reduce corvée labor requires halting construction projects, declining tribute from distant regions, and strictly regulating the postal relay…

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:

匱徭役減而民力不窮始可以言富民矣臣請以教
民之道言之
國家學校之設已有定矣明倫理重廉節則
今日教民之所當急也然欲倫理之明在於脩三物之
教表孝弟之人嚴尊卑之分謹男女之別欲廉節之
重在於獎恬退之士抑奔競之徒厚忠直之賞嚴貪
汙之罰倫理明而百姓以親廉節重而士風以美始
可以言教民矣然立政用賢王道所不可偏廢者政
事雖善而用非其人亦終於無成故富民又在於慎
===
擇守令教民又在於慎擇師儒使為守令者皆如黃
霸卓茂其人則稅斂不患不輕徭役不患不減為師
儒者皆如陽城胡瑗其人則倫理不患不明廉節不
患不重而又擇監司以察守令師儒之臧否擇宰相
以權監司之黜陟則王道之行也有以極其至而治
化之盛也將無以異於古矣雖然善政之所以立賢
才之所以用非
陛下心正身脩其何以為之本哉蓋表必端其影斯直源
必潔其流斯清苟心有萬一之不正而身有萬一之

才之所以用非

必潔其流斯清苟心有萬一之不正而身有萬一之
未脩則政事雖善而一有以妨吾之欲雖善未必行
punctuated:
傳之給，謹泛使之差，重私役之罰。稅斂輕而民財不匱，徭役減而民力不窮，始可以言富民矣。臣請以教民之道言之：國家學校之設已有定矣，明倫理、重廉節，則今日教民之所當急也。然欲倫理之明，在於脩三物之教，表孝弟之人，嚴尊卑之分，謹男女之別；欲廉節之重，在於獎恬退之士，抑奔競之徒，厚忠直之賞，嚴貪汙之罰。倫理明而百姓以親，廉節重而士風以美，始可以言教民矣。然立政用賢，王道所不可偏廢者。政事雖善，而用非其人，亦終於無成。故富民又在於慎擇守令，教民又在於慎擇師儒。使為守令者皆如黃霸、卓茂其人，則稅斂不患不輕，徭役不患不減；為師儒者皆如陽城、胡瑗其人，則倫理不患不明，廉節不患不重。而又擇監司以察守令師儒之臧否，擇宰相以權監司之黜陟，則王道之行也有以極其至，而治化之盛也將無以異於古矣。

雖然，善政之所以立，賢才之所以用，非陛下心正身脩，其何以為之本哉？蓋表必端，其影斯直；源必潔，其流斯清。苟心有萬一之不正，而身有萬一之未脩，則政事雖善，而一有以妨吾之欲，雖善未必行，
translation_en:
…strictly regulate the provisioning of the postal relay service, exercise care in dispatching miscellaneous emissaries, and increase the penalties for requisitioning labor for private purposes. Only when taxation is light and the people's resources are not depleted, and labor service is reduced and their strength is not exhausted, can one speak of enriching the people. Your servant now asks leave to discuss the way to educate the people. The state's arrangements for establishing schools are already fixed. Clarifying ethical relationships and honoring integrity and moral principle are therefore the urgent tasks in educating the people today. To clarify ethical relationships, however, requires cultivating instruction in the three subjects—virtues, conduct, and arts—honoring people who show filial piety and fraternal respect, strictly maintaining the distinctions between superior and inferior, and carefully observing the separation between men and women. To honor integrity and moral principle requires rewarding scholars content to withdraw from advancement, restraining those who scramble for office, generously rewarding loyalty and uprightness, and severely punishing corruption. Only when ethical relationships are clear and the common people consequently live in affection, and integrity and moral principle are honored and the conduct of scholars consequently improves, can one speak of educating the people. Yet establishing sound government and employing the worthy are both indispensable to the kingly Way; neither may be neglected. However good the policies, if those employed are unsuitable, nothing will ultimately be accomplished. Thus enriching the people also depends on carefully selecting prefects and county magistrates, and educating the people also depends on carefully selecting scholarly teachers. If all prefects and county magistrates were men like Huang Ba and Zhuo Mao, there would be no fear that taxation would fail to become lighter or labor service fail to be reduced. If all scholarly teachers were men like Yang Cheng and Hu Yuan, there would be no fear that ethical relationships would fail to become clear or integrity and moral principle fail to be honored. If, moreover, surveillance commissioners were selected to scrutinize the merits and faults of prefects, county magistrates, and scholarly teachers, and chief councilors were selected to weigh the demotion and promotion of surveillance commissioners, the practice of the kingly Way could reach its fullest realization, and the flourishing of good government and moral transformation would be no different from that of antiquity.

Nevertheless, unless Your Majesty's mind is rectified and your person cultivated, what foundation can there be for establishing good government and employing worthy talent? For only when the gnomon is upright will its shadow be straight; only when the source is clean will its stream be clear. If there is even the slightest lack of rectitude in the mind or the slightest deficiency in personal cultivation, then, however good a policy may be, should it in any way obstruct one's desires, its goodness will not ensure that it is implemented…

title: 弘治六年進士登科錄
text:
賢才雖用而一有以拂吾之私雖用未必乆此臣之
論致治成化所以斷然以全天德為之本也仰惟
陛下日御經筵緝熈
聖學其於正心脩身之說聞之熟矣顧所以實用其功者
則臣来自疎遠有所不能與知

===

獻臣聞之賈誼曰習與正人居之不能無正猶生長於
齊不能不齊言也習與不正人居之不能無不正猶
生長於楚之地不能不楚言也夫所謂正人者言依
仁義動由規矩有忠愛之實有匡救之誠所謂不正
人者制行姦回宅心頗僻逢迎以為說阿狥以為容
陛下試以臣之所言驗之平日之所與居者果正人乎果
非正人乎驗其果正人也則引而親之與之謀謨治
道講論經史使之因時啓沃随物箴規如其非正必
斥而遠之使彼之邪諂無所投而吾之聰明無所惑

人者制行燕回宅心頗僻逢迎以為說阿狥以為容
陛下試以臣之所言驗之平日之所與居者果正人乎果
非正人乎驗其果正人也則引而親之與之謀謨諸
道講論經史使之因時啓沃隨物箴規如其非正必
斥而遠之使彼之邪媚無所投而吾之聰明無所惑
punctuated:
賢才雖用，而一有以拂吾之私，雖用未必乆。此臣之論致治成化，所以斷然以全天德為之本也。仰惟陛下日御經筵，緝熈聖學，其於正心脩身之說聞之熟矣。顧所以實用其功者，則臣来自疎遠，有所不能與知。陛下必欲舉行王道，富教斯民，舍此無以用其力矣。臣愚伏願陛下親君子，遠小人，以為正心脩身之助；崇敬畏，戒逸欲，謹言行，正威儀，以實用正心脩身之功。不有其助，則心身固無正脩之理；苟非實用數者之功，又何以為正脩也哉？臣於數者，請得而條陳之，以為終篇獻。
臣聞之，賈誼曰：「習與正人居之，不能無正，猶生長於齊，不能不齊言也；習與不正人居之，不能無不正，猶生長於楚之地，不能不楚言也。」夫所謂正人者，言依仁義，動由規矩，有忠愛之實，有匡救之誠。所謂不正人者，制行姦回，宅心頗僻，逢迎以為說，阿狥以為容。陛下試以臣之所言驗之，平日之所與居者，果正人乎？果非正人乎？驗其果正人也，則引而親之，與之謀謨治道，講論經史，使之因時啓沃，随物箴規。如其非正，必斥而遠之，使彼之邪諂無所投，而吾之聰明無所惑。
translation_en:
…Even when worthy men are employed, if anything they do conflicts with one's private interests, their employment may not last. This is why, in discussing how to achieve good government and bring moral transformation to fruition, your servant firmly takes preserving the wholeness of Heaven-endowed virtue as the foundation. I respectfully reflect that Your Majesty daily attends the Classics Colloquium and continually illuminates your sagely learning. You have often heard the teaching of rectifying the mind and cultivating the self. Yet as to how you actually apply yourself to this work, your servant comes from a remote place and cannot know all its particulars. If Your Majesty is determined to put the Kingly Way into practice and enrich and educate this people, there is no other way to direct your efforts. Your ignorant servant humbly wishes that Your Majesty would draw near to noble men and keep petty men at a distance, to aid in rectifying your mind and cultivating yourself; uphold reverence and awe, guard against indolence and desire, be circumspect in speech and conduct, and make your bearing correct, thereby putting this work into actual practice. Without such assistance, there can surely be no rectification of the mind or cultivation of the self. And unless you actually exert yourself in these several matters, how can rectification and cultivation be accomplished? Allow your servant to set them forth individually as an offering to conclude this essay.
Your servant has heard Jia Yi say: “One who habitually lives among upright people cannot fail to become upright, just as one raised in Qi cannot fail to speak the language of Qi. One who habitually lives among people who are not upright cannot fail to become unrighteous, just as one raised in the land of Chu cannot fail to speak the language of Chu.” Those called upright base their words on benevolence and righteousness and guide their actions by proper standards. Their loyalty and affection are genuine, and their wish to correct faults and remedy errors is sincere. Those called unrighteous are deceitful and perverse in conduct, biased and crooked at heart. They seek to please through flattery and to gain acceptance through obsequious compliance. Let Your Majesty test your everyday companions against what your servant has said: are they truly upright, or are they not? If you find them truly upright, draw them close and treat them with intimacy. Deliberate with them on the way of governing and discuss the classics and histories, letting them enlighten your mind as occasions arise and offer admonition as matters present themselves. If they are not upright, you must dismiss them and keep them at a distance, so that their wicked flattery finds no opening and your own discernment suffers no confusion.
